Learning Objectives
Assess the epidemiology of, etiology of, and risk factors associated with osteochondritis
dissecans.
Outline the presentation patterns and work up of patients in whom osteochondritis dissecans
of the knee, elbow, or ankle is suspected.
Identify the characteristics of and classify osteochondritis dissecans lesions on radiographs
and MRIs.
Specify the natural history of osteochondritis dissecans and identify possible locations of
osteochondritis dissecans in young athletes.
Apply the principles of management to individual lesions.

Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Osteochondritis dissecans (OCD) is an idiopathic focal lesion of subchondral bone. Dissimilar
from osteoarthritis, joint cartilage is affected later in the disease process.
The knee, ankle, and elbow are the most commonly affected joints.
OCD is more common in young athletes with an open physis; the term juvenile OCD also is
used for this age group.
The prognosis of OCD in children and adolescents is more favorable compared with that in
skeletally mature adults.
Nonsurgical treatment results in a higher success rate in young patients; however, surgical
treatment is required in patients with unstable lesions, such as those with a break in the
articular cartilage, and patients who progress or fail to heal despite nonsurgical treatment.
Despite a better prognosis and response to nonsurgical treatment in skeletally immature
patients, long-term outcomes remain variable. Contemporary techniques have been
developed to preserve or restore the articular cartilage.
Epidemiology
The knee is the most common site of OCD in growing children.
The incidence of knee OCD is estimated to be 9.5 to 29 per 100,000; however, the actual
incidence may be higher than that recorded because no studies have confirmed the
radiographic incidence of OCD in large populations of asymptomatic children.

OCD is an acquired lesion of subchondral bone characterized by varying degrees of resorption,
fragmentation, and osteonecrosis that may lead to involvement of the overlying cartilage. OCD
should be distinguished from the normal process of epiphyseal ossification. Normal
epiphyseal ossification is characterized by its typical location at the posterior aspect of the
femoral condyles.
Age and level of skeletal maturity at onset are considered prognostic. In general, children with
closed growth plates at symptom onset have a poorer prognosis.

Epidemiology
OCD is a relatively common source of knee pain and dysfunction and is more common in
children and adolescents aged 10 to 20 years.1 Boys are up to four times more likely to
be affected, and patients aged 12 to 19 years have a twofold higher risk compared with
patients aged 6 to 11 years.2 The overall incidence of knee OCD is estimated at 9.5 to 29
per 100,000.2 Similar to many musculoskeletal disorders of childhood, the actual
incidence of OCD is believed to be much higher. Several studies have suggested that the
incidence of OCD is increasing; however, whether this is a true increase in incidence
because of increased sports participation or identification of more lesions because of
increased awareness by families, coaches, and physicians remains unclear.3
OCD of the ankle is less common than OCD of the knee, with an incidence of 4.6 per
100,000 among children and adolescents aged 6 to 19 years.4 Adolescents aged 12 to 19-
years have an approximately sixfold higher risk compared with patients aged 6 to 11
years. Despite limited data, current evidence suggests that, in contrast to the knee,
females have a twofold higher risk or OCD of the ankle compared with males.
The incidence of OCD of the elbow is 2.2 per 100,000. Patients aged 12 to 19 years have
an almost 22 times higher risk of elbow OCD compared with patients aged 6 to 11 years.
Males have a sevenfold higher risk compared with females. Knee and ankle OCD lesions
do not often demonstrate a clear left-right predilection; however, almost two-thirds of
elbow OCD is diagnosed on the right side (related to hand dominance).5

Panner disease is a distinct entity and is an osteochondrosis similar to Legg-Calvé-
Perthes disease of the hip. Panner disease often is observed in males younger than 10
years. Patients with Panner disease respond well to nonsurgical treatment, including
activity restrictions. The true incidence of Panner disease is unknown.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
OCD of the medial femoral condyle is most common, followed by the lateral femoral condyle
and the patella. Tibial involvement is rare.
Altered biomechanics appear to play a role in OCD of the knee. Marked knee valgus
predisposes patients to lateral lesions, and marked knee varus predisposes patients to medial
lesions.6
In the ankle, the most common site is the medial dome of the talus, followed by the lateral
talus.
Almost all OCD lesions of the elbow occur in the capitellum. The biomechanical forces affecting
the capitellum have been more well described than those of the knee and ankle. Valgus stress
on the elbow is a major contributor to development of the disease.
Panner disease always affects the capitellum, and biomechanical alterations and increased
valgus stress play a role in its development.

Osteology
The medial femoral condyle is the most common site for OCD overall and in the knee
(60% to 70%). The lateral aspect of the medial femoral condyle is at the highest risk,
presumably because of the higher shear forces incurred during activity. Lateral femoral
condyle OCD lesions also are common and constitute approximately one-third of knee
lesions. Patellar lesions are substantially less common than condylar lesions.
Involvement of the femoral trochlea and the tibial plafond is rare.
Some evidence suggests that lateral lesions are more common in knees with increased
valgus and that medial lesions are more common in knees with increased varus.6,7 Other

biomechanical alterations that increase load and, therefore, may predispose the knee to
OCD include meniscectomy, joint instability, greater posterior tibial slope, and femoral
condylar flattening. Abnormal patellar surface anatomy and patellofemoral maltracking
may increase the risk of patellar OCD.1
Medial talar lesions are twice as common as lateral OCD lesions. Central talar dome and
tibial plafond lesions are exceedingly rare.
In the elbow, almost all OCD occurs in the capitellum (97% to 100%); however, lesions of
the radial head, trochlea, and olecranon also have been reported.8 With most lesions
occurring in the dominant arm of throwing athletes, the role of altered biomechanics in
elbow OCD is better understood than that of the knee and ankle. The capitellum
transmits more than 60% of the compressive force on the elbow, and the considerable
valgus torque generated during throwing movements is a substantial contributor to the
development of elbow OCD.9 Injuries to the ulnar collateral ligament of the elbow also
increase the risk of capitellar OCD by subjecting the lateral compartment of the elbow to
undue stress.
Etiology
The pathogenesis of OCD is multifactorial and not fully understood; however, subchondral
bone ischemia/repetitive microtrauma are believed to be contributing factors in the
development of OCD. These underlying conditions lead to subsequent changes to the
biomechanical properties of the bone/cartilage complex, which result in a wide spectrum of
pathologies of the bone and cartilage.
Causes of subchondral bone ischemia may be grouped into mechanical and biologic factors.
Mechanical etiologic factors include injury, overuse, and biomechanical alterations. In the
knee, meniscal pathologies and tibial spine impingement have been postulated as other site-
specific factors.
Biologic etiologies include genetic factors, defects in ossification centers (especially of the
distal femur), and endocrine abnormalities.
Obesity also has been linked to OCD. Moderate obesity increases the risk of knee OCD,
whereas extreme obesity increases the risk of knee, elbow, and ankle OCD.10,11


Etiology
The underlying etiology of OCD has been the subject of several animal and human
studies. OCD is the result of a complex, multifactorial process. The specific contribution
of each factor to the etiology of OCD remains unclear. The immediate cause of the
pathologic process of OCD appears to be ischemia/fracture of the subchondral bone.
Dissimilar from osteonecrosis, which frequently involves large portions of the bone, the
process in OCD is focal and smaller. The causes of this ischemia and changes to
subchondral bone could be categorized as biologic and mechanical factors.
Historically, mechanical factors have been proposed to be causally related to OCD since
the earliest reports of the entity. Acute macrotrauma rarely has been linked to OCD,
whereas repetitive microtrauma and mechanical loading of the joint is likely. The
interplay of chronic microtrauma and other mechanical and biologic factors is the most
commonly cited etiology of OCD.
Altered biomechanical loading on the joint is an important contributor to abnormal
forces on the bone and increases the likelihood of OCD. This correlation has been
established more clearly in the elbow and knee; however, some evidence for the ankle
also exists. Angular deformities of the knee joint, meniscal pathologies, abnormal
condylar anatomy, ligamentous insufficiency (including congenial absence of knee
ligaments), and patellofemoral pathologies have been linked to OCD. In the elbow,
cubitus valgus, insufficiency of medial structures (ulnar collateral ligament, medial
epicondyle), and radiocapitellar joint pathologies have been associated with OCD.
Biologic factors have gained increasing attention as the etiology of OCD in the past two
decades. Several cases of familial occurrence of OCD (typically of the knee) have led
researchers to explore the potential role of genetics in the development of OCD lesions.
Several genes have been studied, and mutations of the ACAN gene (which encodes an
extracellular matrix protein) and type IX collagen have been found in some
patients.1,12,13 Although genetics appears to play a role in some patients with OCD, most
patients do not have known genetic abnormalities.

Hormonal imbalances, including low vitamin D3 levels, growth hormone abnormalities,
and other bone metabolism disorders, have been linked to OCD.
Obesity also has been linked to OCD. Patients with OCD of the knee, elbow, and ankle
have a higher body mass index (BMI) (absolute and percentile). Patients with moderate
obesity (BMI greater than or equal to the ninety-fifth percentile for age or BMI ≥30
kg/m2) have a nearly twofold increased risk of knee OCD. Extreme obesity (BMI ≥1.2 ×
ninety-fifth percentile for age or BMI ≥35 kg/m2) substantially increases the risk of knee,
elbow, and ankle OCD10,11 (Figure 1).

Natural History
The natural history of OCD is not well understood; however, evidence supports the notion that
juvenile OCD has a substantially more favorable natural history and prognosis compared with
adult OCD.
The natural history of Panner disease is quite favorable. Almost all patients respond to
nonsurgical treatment, and the lesion usually resolves in 6 to 12 months.
Classification
Multiple classification systems are available for evaluating OCD lesions.
Plain radiographs, MRI, and arthroscopic classification schemes have been introduced.
The most important distinction to be made in the evaluation of patients with OCD is whether
the lesion is stable or unstable, which will guide treatment decisions in all joints.

Classification
Several classification systems have been proposed for OCD. These classification systems
are based on plain radiographs, MRIs, or the arthroscopic appearance of the lesion.
Although the rater performance characteristics of these classification systems vary, the
common goal is to evaluate the stability of the lesion. Stable lesions generally are
amenable to an initial period of nonsurgical management, whereas unstable lesions are
less likely to heal via nonsurgical management.
The radiographic classification system for ankle OCD described by Berndt and Hardy14
was introduced in 1959 (Table 1). Stage 1 lesions are intact, stable, and only show
increased density of the subchondral bone on radiographs. Stage 2 lesions are partially
detached, whereas stage 3 lesions are fully detached but remain in situ. Stage 4 indicates
a completely detached, mobile fragment or a loose body.

terminology stable/unstable has been replaced with immobile/mobile, which is more
accurate in describing the characteristics of a lesion on arthroscopic probing (Figure 2).

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Clinical Presentation
Patients with OCD typically have two distinct types of presentations.
The OCD may be an incidental finding observed on radiographs obtained for unrelated
reasons or it may be the primary finding in a patient with months-long nonspecific activity-
related pain with or without a history of trauma.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:29 PM
AAOS | Osteochondritis Dissecans and Panner Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004065
11/35

Patients typically present with generalized knee pain (often anterior) and variable swelling with
or without prior trauma. Onset may be associated with an increase or change in activity.
Careful assessment can clarify whether symptoms include pain or mechanical popping and
locking to determine appropriate management.

Clinical Presentation
Knee pain is a common complaint in children and adolescents. Given the high rate of
asymptomatic lesions, many OCD lesions are found incidentally on radiographs. Another
common presentation is months-long unspecific knee pain. The pain is most commonly
vague and generalized but also may be localized to the anterior knee or the medial side
of the knee. Pain usually is aggravated by physical activity and sports participation;
however, a specific history of a traumatic event typically is not present. Because of the
vague, mild pain and often waxing-waning symptoms, most patients have prolonged
symptoms before a lesion is diagnosed, which one study reported to be as long as 14
months from symptom onset.17
Substantial symptoms, including moderate to severe pain, locking, popping, and giving
way, are experienced by a subset of patients. Effusion is a less common symptom,
occurring in approximately 20% of patients.18
The clinical presentation of patients with elbow and ankle OCD is similar to that of
patients with knee OCD. In ankle lesions, surgeons must differentiate OCD from an
osteochondral fracture of the talus, which is a separate entity. Osteochondral fractures
are more commonly related to an acute traumatic event and are more common on the
lateral talus compared with OCD, which is more common on the medial side.
Physical Examination
A thorough physical examination is necessary to identify any comorbid conditions, such as
meniscal tears, loose bodies, or instability.

Deep pressure over the medial parapatellar area may produce pain if the knee is flexed but
not if the knee is extended.
Application of varus or valgus stress throughout a full range of motion may produce reports of
pain and popping if a medial or lateral femoral condylar fragment is sufficiently loose.
In addition, patients with an elbow lesion may have a positive radiocapitellar compression test
with an extended elbow.

Physical Examination
Although physical examination often is not specific in the diagnosis of OCD, it is an
indispensable tool in patients in whom an OCD lesion is suspected and to evaluate the
joint for stability. A thorough physical examination of the knee, elbow, or ankle for
possible ligamentous pathologies is imperative because concurrent ligamentous injuries
and OCD are not uncommon and both should be addressed for a successful outcome.
Bauer17 described a physical examination for knee lesions, which may help identify
lesions of the lateral aspect of the medial femoral condyle. This maneuver involves
flexing the knee to 90°, and then extending the knee to 30° while externally rotating the
tibia. Pain at the anteromedial knee is considered a positive test. This test is neither
sensitive nor specific and is helpful only in the classic location of OCD.19,20
Deep palpation of the anteromedial ankle may elicit pain in patients with an ankle lesion.
Capitellar OCD may be accompanied by tenderness to direct palpation of the lateral
elbow. In addition, patients with an elbow lesion may have a positive radiocapitellar
compression test; this test is positive if pain is present in supination and pronation with
an extended elbow.
Imaging Studies
Radiography

Imaging studies are the first step in diagnosing OCD. If appropriate views are obtained, plain
radiographs are acceptable for the diagnosis of OCD.
Standard weight-bearing AP, lateral, tunnel, and Merchant views should be obtained for knee
lesions.
An OCD lesion in the classic position on the lateral aspect of the medial femoral condyle may
be overlooked on an AP view in extension because of overriding bone.
Classic lesions are best visualized on a tunnel view.
Elbow: standard AP view with the elbow extended, lateral view, and a 45° AP flexion view
Ankle: standard AP, lateral, and mortise views

Radiography
The goal of imaging studies for OCD in any location is twofold: to diagnose the lesion,
which may be small in size and location, making it more challenging to visualize; and to
determine prognostic information to guide management. Therefore, plain radiographs
are the first diagnostic step in the evaluation of a patient in whom OCD is suspected.
Plain radiographs should be evaluated for OCD location, concomitant bony pathology,
and skeletal maturity, which are substantial prognostic factors.
In the knee, four radiographic views should be obtained, including weight-bearing AP,
lateral, tunnel, and Merchant views. The classic location for knee OCD is the lateral
aspect of the medial femoral condyle, which may be missed on an AP view because of
overriding bone. An OCD at the classic location is tangential to the x-ray beam on a
tunnel view; therefore, is the preferred radiographic view for this lesion. A Merchant or
sunrise view is invaluable in evaluating suspected trochlear or patellar lesions.
Radiographs of the contralateral side also may be considered because asymptomatic
lesions of the contralateral knee have been reported in 20% to 30% of patients in some
series. Coronal malalignment of the lower limbs is a potential contributor to knee OCD;
therefore, in patients with clinical malalignment, long-leg standing radiographs are
ordered to determine the severity of varus/valgus, which occasionally requires
correction.

In younger patients (especially those <10 years), the distal femur ossification center may
show changes similar to those of OCD, which are considered normal variants. To avoid
confusing this normal variant with OCD, surgeons should remember that knee OCD is
rare in children younger than 9 years, and the normal variant most commonly involves
the lateral condyle, whereas knee OCD is more common on the medial side (Figure 3).

immature patient demonstrate an osteochondritis dissecans lesion of the lateral aspect
of the medial femoral condyle. Often, lesions are best observed on a notch/tunnel view.
(Courtesy of Theodore J. Ganley, MD, Philadelphia, PA.)
Imaging studies for elbow OCD involve an AP view with the elbow extended, a lateral
view, and a 45° flexed AP view. The utility of plain radiographs is lower in the diagnosis of
elbow OCD compared with knee OCD, which may be because of smaller lesion size or
the anatomy of the capitellum. Findings include sclerosis, subchondral lucency,
fragmentation, and capitellar flattening.
Panner disease is relatively easy to diagnose on plain radiographs because it involves a
large portion of the capitellum and occurs in an age group with a very low incidence of
elbow OCD (Figure 4).

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Plain radiographs are appropriate for OCD lesions that are in classic locations, well
visualized on plain radiographs, and milder in severity and amenable to healing via
nonsurgical management. MRI is the preferred imaging modality for evaluating OCD
lesions of the knee, ankle, and elbow in atypical locations and for larger lesions that
may be managed surgically.
MRI is valuable is determining the exact location and size of the lesion. It also may be
helpful in patients with a moderately advanced lesion to provide an estimate of lesion
stability short of arthroscopic examination.

A high intensity signal line between the lesion and the surrounding bone on a T2-
weighted MRI is a specific sign of lesion instability. In addition, breaks in the articular
cartilage, fissuring, the water content of the cartilage, and the presence of
subchondral cysts can be evaluated on MRI.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI has supplanted bone scanning in the evaluation of OCD and is the
preferred imaging modality if a lesion is found on plain radiographs and more
advanced analysis is required. The size, location, and stability of the lesion can
be evaluated via MRI. Because stability of the lesion determines management,
the indicators of instability should assessed on MRI. De Smet et al15 have
described four findings that may help identify stable and unstable lesions, which
should be evaluated on T2-weighted MRIs: (1) high intensity signal line between
the lesion and the surrounding bone, (2) focal defect in the articular cartilage, (3)
fracture of the overlying cartilage, and (4) subchondral cysts. The first criterion is
the most specific predictor of instability.
Although the sensitivity of MRI in the diagnosis unstable lesions is near 100%,
the specificity of MRI is low in younger patients with open physes. The highest
specificity has been noted in skeletally mature patients; however, a high number
of OCD lesions in skeletally immature children that are diagnosed as unstable
on MRI are deemed stable on arthroscopic examination (Resource 1; Figures 5
and 6).

Pathology

Pathology
Subchondral osteonecrosis is the characteristic sign of OCD. The initial change is
necrosis of the bone, which is then absorbed and replaced by creeping substitution.
During the healing stage, the overlying cartilage is biomechanically weak and prone to
injury, which may lead to progression of the lesion, cartilage separation, and loose
bodies.
Management
Several factors must be considered in devising a treatment plan for the management of OCD
in young athletes, the most important of which are skeletal maturity and the stability of the
lesion. Younger patients with wide-open physes have the best likelihood of a favorable
outcome with nonsurgical treatment, whereas skeletally mature patients have a higher risk for
failed nonsurgical treatment and the need for surgical treatment.
Nonsurgical Management
Patients of any age with a stable lesion are initially treated via rest, activity restrictions, anti-
inflammatory medications, and pain modalities as necessary.
No universally agreed upon protocol for nonsurgical management exists; however, nonsurgical
treatment regimens described previously include rest, bracing, cast immobilization, and/or
weight-bearing limitations.


Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management typically is the initial treatment option for skeletally immature
patients with a stable lesion. Although minimal agreement exists with regard to the
optimal nonsurgical treatment protocol, the main principle is to avoid high-impact sports
and encourage the patient to modify activities to ensure minimal trauma to the joint.
Activity modifications may be supplemented with immobilization, which may include the
use of a brace or cast for as long as 6 weeks. Physical therapy and strengthening also
may be considered. The preferred nonsurgical treatment option of the authors of the
lesson for the management knee OCD includes unloader bracing and home exercises
that involve core strengthening, straight leg raises, and hamstring and quadriceps
stretching for 3 months, with activity restrictions to avoid high-impact running or
jumping. Patients with lesions that demonstrate evidence of radiographic healing are
advanced to a physical therapy rehabilitation program.
Close follow-up is an integral aspect of the nonsurgical management of OCD.
Radiographs are simple to obtain and, therefore, are the preferred imaging modality for
assessing response to management. Plain radiographs are associated with excellent
reliability in assessment of overall healing of femoral OCD.21 As many as two-thirds of
patients have a good response to nonsurgical treatment and progress to healing with as
many as 6 months of treatment.22 Prognostic factors that indicate a lower likelihood of
healing with nonsurgical management are closed physes, larger lesion size (especially
coronal width), subchondral cysts, and mechanical symptoms. Surgical management is
recommended if a lesion fails to respond to nonsurgical management for 6 months.
Longer durations of nonsurgical treatment are not only inconvenient for an active child
but also unlikely to lead to healing.
Ankle OCD also is managed via rest and activity modifications. A short leg cast is
recommended for 6 to 8 weeks, after which physical therapy may be initiated. Activity
restrictions should be continued for at least 6 months. For ankle lesions, some surgeons
recommend prolonged nonsurgical management for as long as 1 year. Approximately
one-half of skeletally immature patients respond well to nonsurgical treatment of 1-year
duration.

The same principles are applied in patients with elbow OCD. Patients with a stable lesion
are treated via rest and activity modifications. The patient is advised to refrain from any
aggravating activities, throwing movements, and weight lifting. Immobilization is not
favored; however, physical therapy to focus on range-of-motion exercises and
strengthening is encouraged. Patients with wide-open physes and intact lesions who
comply with this protocol likely progress to healing, which has been reported in as many
as 85% of patients.23 Similar to the knee, 6 months typically is considered the limit of
nonsurgical management. Although all patients are unique, if healing does not occur
after 6 months, then surgical treatment typically is advised. Patients with an unstable
lesion, patients with associated motion loss, patients with closed physes, and patients
with a large lesion are candidates for early surgical treatment.
Nonsurgical management is the preferred treatment option for Panner disease. Patients
generally respond to a few weeks of activity restrictions, and most patients are
asymptomatic within 6 to 8 weeks. Return to activity should begin gradually to prevent
recurrent pain and discomfort.
Surgical Management
Indications for surgical management include failure to respond to nonsurgical management,
detached or unstable lesions, continued pain and symptoms despite lack of evidence of
progression, and loose bodies.
The goals of surgical management are maintenance of articular cartilage congruity, fixation of
unstable fragments, and repair of cartilage defects.
Two main categories of surgical treatment options are available.
Those performed to induce and promote healing, which may be supplemented with fixation.
The goals of these treatment options are to preserve the native cartilage.
Salvage procedures that are performed in patients with loose bodies, degenerative cartilage,
unfixable lesions, or bare subchondral bone
Although preoperative planning is vital for successful outcomes, the final decision with regard
to surgical technique is made on arthroscopic examination of the lesion.
Stable lesions are amenable to extra-articular or trans-articular arthroscopic drilling. Drilling
for stable OCD lesions should be performed slowly so excessive heat does not cause bone or
cartilage damage. During trans-articular drilling, the knee should be flexed and extended

Unstable lesions are managed via arthroscopic or open débridement and fixation. In young
adolescents, fixation of unstable lesions should be attempted. Bioabsorbable or metal fixation
materials may be used but should be placed deep to the articular cartilage.
Loose fragments that can be fixed should be retained and secured with the use of pins and/or
screws. Fragments that do not fit within the bone defect or are severely damaged should be
removed, after which chondroplasty or a cartilage restoration procedure is performed.

Surgical Management
In young athletes, the main indication for surgical treatment is failure of a lesion to
respond to nonsurgical management for 3 to 6 months. The decision to proceed with
surgical management also may depend on the size of the lesion and patient symptoms.
Other indications include unstable or detached lesions and loose bodies. In addition,
patients who have substantial symptoms during the course of nonsurgical treatment,
despite lack of evidence for progression of disease, may be considered candidates for
surgical management. Surgical treatment is performed to promote healing in patients
with an intact or stable lesion, provide rigid fixation in patients with an unstable lesion,
and restore the congruity of the joint by replacing the damaged cartilage with a similar
tissue in patients with an unrepairable lesion.
Lesions with intact cartilage are amenable to arthroscopic drilling, which may be
performed from the arthroscopic portals (trans-articular approach) or from the epiphysis
without penetrating the joint (retroarticular approach; Figure 7). Both techniques are
acceptable given the lesion is visualized and identified, multiple drilling of the
subchondral bone is performed, and care is taken to not overheat bone and cause
additional damage. Retroarticular drilling is associated with the theoretic advantage of
avoiding joint cartilage penetration; however, retroarticular drilling of lesions in locations
other than that of the classic lesion (lateral aspect of the medial femoral condyle) is
technically challenging. If the lesion is deemed unstable on arthroscopic examination, a
form of fixation is used to secure the lesion in situ (Resource 2).

Unstable lesions should undergo rigid fixation. Several options are available for fixation,
including mini-fragment screws, headless screws, bioabsorbable pins and screws, and
osteochondral plugs. All techniques are acceptable given that rigid fixation of the lesion
is achieved, the cartilage does not have step-offs or does not subside after fixation, and
the hardware is flush with or deep to the cartilage (Figures 8 and 9). Although
bioabsorbable implants appear more appealing, they have been linked to synovitis,
chronic effusion, and osteolysis in some patient. If cysts and poor bone quality are
present deep to the cartilage, the lesion is removed, curettage and bone grafting is
performed, and the lesion is rigidly fixed (Video 1).

Despite all efforts, some lesions are not amenable to fixation. Indications for removal of
OCD include loose bodies that do not fit within the parent bone defect, cartilage
fragmentation, and poor cartilage quality. To restore joint congruity, some form of
cartilage restoration procedure should be considered.
Drilling to stimulate the underlying bone marrow (ie, marrow stimulation) is similar to
drilling of intact OCD, except that it is performed on exposed subchondral bone. The
goal is to promote fibrocartilage over the exposed defect. Despite short-term alleviation
of pain and symptoms, the tissue described is not conducive to the long-term health of
the joint in patients with a large lesion managed in this fashion. Therefore, only small

Several techniques are available to restore articular cartilage in patients with a full-
thickness cartilage defect. Autologous osteochondral plugs from non–weight-bearing
areas of the femoral condyle can be used to fill the defect. Results generally are
favorable for small- to intermediate-size lesions. This technique is challenging in larger
defects if multiple plugs are used because of the challenges of matching the contour of
the adjacent cartilage with the use of multiple plugs and donor-site morbidity with the
use of multiple plugs.
Fresh-frozen osteochondral allograft transplantation may be considered in larger lesions
(Video 2; Figure 10). This technique can be used as a primary treatment option for
extremely large lesions or as a salvage, secondary procedure in lesions that did not heal
via less-invasive surgical management. The results are favorable in most patients, with a
substantial reduction in pain and disability and return to sports in most children.24,25

Autologous chondrocyte implantation is another technique with indications and
outcomes similar to those of osteochondral allograft transplantation (Figure 11). As a
two-stage procedure, a patient’s own cartilage tissue is harvested and cultured and then
implanted to regenerate the hyaline cartilage that was missing. Similar to allograft
transplantation, this technique can be used in large (>2 cm2), contained, full-thickness
cartilage defects. The main limitation with this technique is the depth of subchondral
bone involvement. Outcomes are similar to those of osteochondral allograft
transplantation, with most patients regaining reasonable function and activity levels.

For knee lesions, concurrent coronal plane deformity should be assessed clinically or
radiographically. The indications to surgically correct these deformities are unclear;
however, the role of coronal malalignment may be more pronounced in patients with
recalcitrant lesions. Surgical correction of malalignment can be undertaken at the same
time as primary or secondary OCD surgery or can be staged, depending on surgeon
preference.
The same treatment principles applied to ankle and elbow OCD. Similar techniques with
minor modifications are used; however, because of the small size of elbow lesions and
other concerns, autologous chondrocyte implantation is not routinely used in the elbow.
Instead, osteochondral autograft or allograft transplantation is performed (Figure 12;
Videos 3 and 4).

The postoperative rehabilitation protocol largely depends on the joint (upper versus
lower extremity) and the procedure performed. For ankle and knee lesions, weight-
bearing restrictions typically are continued for 6 weeks, with the patient walking with
crutches and toe-touch weight bearing. Physical therapy is of utmost importance
postoperatively, with an emphasis on active-assisted and passive range of motion
initially, followed by quadriceps activation and strengthening. Progression to full–weight
bearing is initiated between 6 and 12 weeks, depending on a patient’s symptoms, with

close follow-up for possible complications. Complete healing of the lesion is not
expected for at least 6 months.
Follow-up MRI is performed 6 months postoperatively to assess healing. Continued
healing is expected for 1 to 2 years, and patients should be followed until then. A gradual
return to sports activity is initiated at least 6 to 9 months postoperatively to ensure
adequate biomechanical strength of the OCD.
Complications of the surgical management of OCD are grouped into two major
categories: complications that result from nonhealing of the lesion or are otherwise
lesion-related and complications that are surgery -related. The first group of
complications is more common, and the management of such complications should be
individualized for each patient. The latter group of complications are less common, and
include infection, arthrofibrosis, hardware irritation or failure, neurovascular
complications of surgical management, and overgrowth of the implanted cartilage from
autologous chondrocyte implantation. Although few studies have been published on the
complications of the surgical management of OCD, the complication rate is low, and
most of the observed complications are related to the progression/nonhealing of the
lesion itself rather than the surgical procedure.
